Going from a text (and other conditions) to a video is just a few lines of code. Below we show how to do text-to-video generation with the LTX-Video model from Lightricks.

The memory requirements for any model can be computed by adding the following:

Memory required by weights can be lowered via - quantization, downcasting to lower dtypes, or by offloading to CPU. Memory required for activations states can also be lowered but that is a more involved process, which is out of the scope of this blog.

It is possible to run any video model with extremely low memory, but it comes at the cost of time required for inference. If the time required by an optimization technique is more than what a user considers reasonable, it is not feasible to run inference. Diffusers provides many such optimizations that are opt-in and can be chained together.

In the table below, we provide the memory requirements for three popular video generation models with reasonable defaults:

These numbers were obtained with the following settings on an 80GB A100 machine (full script here):

These requirements are quite staggering, and make these models difficult to run on consumer hardware. With Diffusers, users can opt-in to different optimizations to reduce memory usage. The following table provides the memory requirements for HunyuanVideo with various optimizations enabled that make minimal compromises on quality and time required for inference.

We used HunyuanVideo for this study, as it is sufficiently large enough, to show the benefits of the optimizations in a progressive manner.

*8Bit models in bitsandbytes cannot be moved to CPU from GPU, unlike the 4Bit ones. ^The memory usage does not reduce further because the peak utilizations come from computing attention and feed-forward. Using Flash Attention and Optimized Feed-Forward can help lower this requirement to ~5 GB.

We used the same settings as above to obtain these numbers. Also note that due to numerical precision loss, quantization can impact the quality of the outputs, effects of which are more prominent in videos than images.

We provide more details about these optimizations in the sections below along with some code snippets to go. But if you're already feeling excited, we encourage you to check out our guide.

Video generation can be quite difficult on resource-constrained devices and time-consuming even on beefier GPUs. Diffusers provides a suite of utilities that help to optimize both the runtime and memory consumption of these models. These optimizations fall under the following categories:

Below, we provide a list of some advanced optimization techniques that are currently work-in-progress and will be merged soon:

Below is an example of applying 4bit quantization, vae tiling, cpu offloading, and layerwise casting to HunyuanVideo to reduce the required VRAM to just ~6.5 GB for 121 x 512 x 768 resolution videos. To the best of our knowledge, this is the lowest memory requirement to run HunyuanVideo among all available implementations without compromising speed.

Install Diffusers from source to try out these features! Some implementations are agnostic to the model being used, and can be applied in other backends easily - be sure to check it out!

We refer the readers to this guide for a detailed take on video generation and the current possibilities in Diffusers.

We’ve created finetrainers - a repository that allows you to easily fine-tune the latest generation of open video models. For example, here is how you would fine-tune CogVideoX with LoRA:

We used finetrainers to emulate the "dissolve" effect and obtained promising results. Check out the model for additional details.

We anticipate significant advancements in video generation models throughout 2025, with major improvements in both output quality and model capabilities. Our goal is to make using these models easy and accessible. We will continue to grow the finetrainers library, and we are planning on adding many more features: Control LoRAs, Distillation Algorithms, ControlNets, Adapters, and more. As always, community contributions are welcome 🤗

Our commitment remains strong to partnering with model publishers, researchers, and community members to ensure the latest innovations in video generation are within reach to everyone.

#10891. How Developers Can Improve Their Learning and Productivity With AI

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how developers learn, write code, and manage their daily work. Tasks that once required hours of searching, testing, and manual effort can now be completed with help from AI. Developers can use it to understand complex programming concepts, find coding errors, learn new technologies, and complete repetitive tasks.

However, AI is not only useful for writing code faster. It can also help developers improve their technical knowledge, solve problems, and build better learning habits. When used correctly, it can become a useful assistant throughout the software development process.

The key is to understand where AI can help and where human skills are still needed. Here are several practical ways developers can use AI to improve their learning and productivity.

Learning a new programming language or understanding a difficult concept can take time. Developers often need to read long explanations, watch tutorials, and test different examples before they understand how something works.

AI can make this process easier by explaining technical concepts in simple language. Instead of searching through several websites, developers can ask direct questions and receive explanations based on their current knowledge.

For example, a developer learning JavaScript can ask AI to explain promises, callbacks, or asynchronous functions. It can break these topics into smaller parts and provide simple code examples to make them easier to understand.

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain the same concept in different ways. If one explanation is difficult to understand, a different example or comparison may make the idea clearer.

AI explanations are not always accurate, especially when dealing with complex programming concepts or unfamiliar technologies. Developers should verify important information before using it in their projects. Hallucination detection can help identify fabricated facts, incorrect technical explanations, and misleading information in AI-generated responses, making it easier to check the accuracy of what they learn.

This helps developers spend less time struggling with unfamiliar topics and more time building their technical knowledge.

Software development changes regularly. New frameworks, libraries, programming languages, and development methods continue to appear. Developers need to keep learning if they want to stay up to date.

AI can support this process by helping developers create learning plans based on their goals and current skills.

For example, a developer who wants to learn Python can ask AI to create a beginner-friendly learning plan. The plan can include basic syntax, variables, loops, functions, object-oriented programming, and small projects.

AI can also recommend practical exercises for each topic. Instead of only reading about a programming concept, developers can write code and test their understanding.

Here are some ways to use AI when learning new technologies:

However, developers should not depend entirely on AI-generated explanations. They should also read official documentation and test examples themselves. This helps them understand how technologies work in real development environments.

AI can help developers improve their coding skills by providing examples, explaining different solutions, and identifying areas that need improvement.

For example, a developer may write a function that works but contains unnecessary steps. They can ask AI to review the code and suggest ways to make it easier to read, maintain, or understand.

AI can also explain why one solution may be better than another. This allows developers to learn different approaches instead of always following the first solution they find.

Some practical ways to use AI for coding improvement include:

Developers can also ask AI to create small coding challenges based on their skill level. For example, someone learning Python can request exercises about lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions.

The important thing is to understand the code instead of copying it without review. Developers who examine the logic behind each solution can improve their programming knowledge over time.

Developers learn new information from many sources, including online courses, technical blogs, documentation, tutorials, and coding projects. Without a proper system, it can become difficult to find useful information when they need it again.

AI can help developers organize this knowledge and make learning resources easier to review.

For example, developers can use AI to summarize long technical explanations, create revision questions, and organize important programming concepts into smaller topics. They can also turn their learning notes into structured study guides that make it easier to revisit important information.

A well-organized knowledge system can be useful when learning a new framework or preparing for technical interviews. Instead of searching through old browser tabs or reading the same documentation repeatedly, developers can return to their saved explanations and notes.

Here are some useful ways to organize technical knowledge:

Technical documentation can contain detailed explanations that are difficult to remember. Developers can use AI to summarize important sections and turn them into short notes.

For example, when learning a new API, they can save information about its main functions, parameters, common errors, and practical examples.

Reading information does not always mean remembering it. Developers can ask AI to create questions from their notes so they can test their understanding.

For example, after learning about database indexing, they can create questions about how indexes work, when to use them, and how they affect query performance.

Developers should also save important information about their projects. This may include coding decisions, API details, database structures, and solutions to common problems.

Keeping these details organized makes it easier to return to a project after a break or help another developer understand the work.

Developers spend a large part of their working time on tasks that do not always require complex problem-solving. These may include writing basic code structures, creating test cases, preparing documentation, and handling repeated coding patterns.

AI can help reduce this manual effort by generating suggestions and automating parts of these tasks.

For example, when starting a new project, developers often need to create similar code structures, such as basic functions, configuration files, and reusable components. An AI coding assistant can generate an initial version that developers can review and adjust.

Automating these activities gives developers more time to focus on important parts of their projects, such as system design, complex features, and problem-solving.

However, generated code should always be checked before it is added to a project. Developers need to make sure it follows project requirements, coding standards, and security rules.

Finding and fixing bugs is an important part of software development. Even experienced developers can spend hours trying to understand why a program is not working as expected.

AI can help make debugging easier by explaining error messages, identifying possible causes, and suggesting solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters a Python error, they can share the relevant code and error message with an AI assistant. The assistant can explain what the error means and suggest possible ways to fix it.

AI can also help developers review code before submitting it. It may identify common issues such as:

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain why a particular bug occurs instead of only requesting a corrected version of the code.

This helps developers understand the problem and avoid making the same mistake in future projects.

Still, AI suggestions are not always correct. Developers should test proposed fixes, review the surrounding code, and confirm that the solution does not introduce new problems.

Managing several development tasks at once can be difficult. Developers may need to work on new features, fix bugs, review code, attend meetings, and meet project deadlines.

AI can help organize these responsibilities by breaking large tasks into smaller and more manageable steps.

For example, if a developer needs to build a user authentication system, they can ask AI to divide the work into separate tasks. These may include creating registration forms, setting up database tables, implementing login logic, adding password protection, and testing the system.

This makes it easier to understand the work involved and decide what needs attention first.

AI can also help explain technical requirements before development begins. This may reduce confusion and help developers identify missing details early.

However, AI-generated plans should be treated as starting points. Developers still need to consider their actual deadlines, technical limitations, and project requirements before following them.

Although AI offers many benefits, depending on it for every programming task can affect a developer's ability to solve problems independently.

If developers always ask AI to write code, fix errors, and explain every concept, they may miss opportunities to develop their own technical skills.

A 2026 Anthropic study found that participants using AI scored 17 percentage points lower on a programming knowledge quiz than participants who worked without AI in the experiment. This highlights why understanding the work still matters when using coding assistants.

Developers can avoid excessive dependence on AI by following a few simple practices:

When facing a coding problem, spend some time understanding it and trying possible solutions. If you get stuck, use AI to explore the issue rather than asking it to complete everything.

Never add AI-generated code to a project without understanding what it does. Review the logic, check the functions, and test the output.

AI can sometimes provide outdated information, incorrect code, or explanations that do not fit a particular project. Check important details against official documentation and reliable technical resources.

Regular coding practice without assistance helps developers maintain their problem-solving skills. It also shows whether they truly understand a programming concept.

The best approach is to use AI as a helpful assistant while keeping independent thinking and technical judgment at the center of development work.

Using AI occasionally can be helpful, but developers can get more value from it by making it part of a regular learning and working routine.

A simple daily routine can help developers balance their project responsibilities with continuous learning.

For example, developers can follow this approach:

Start with a learning goal: Spend some time understanding a new programming concept, framework, or technology. Use AI to explain difficult topics and provide practical examples.

Plan the day's development tasks: Ask AI to help organize important tasks and break complex work into smaller steps.

Use AI during development: Get help with unfamiliar code, debugging, test cases, and repetitive tasks. Review all suggestions before using them.

Save useful information: Keep important explanations, coding examples, and solutions in an organized knowledge base for future reference.

Review what you learned: At the end of the day, revisit important concepts and test your understanding through small questions or coding exercises.

Developers do not need to spend hours following this routine. Even a short period of focused learning each day can help them build knowledge while managing their regular development work.

AI is becoming a useful part of modern software development. It can help developers understand difficult concepts, learn new technologies, improve code quality, debug problems, and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.

However, better productivity does not simply mean writing more code in less time. Developers also need to understand what they are building, improve their problem-solving skills, and keep learning as technology changes.

The most effective approach is to use AI for support rather than letting it make every decision. By combining AI assistance with regular practice, independent thinking, and organized learning, developers can improve both their technical skills and everyday productivity.

#10890. Open-R1: a fully open reproduction of DeepSeek-R1

If you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully. OpenAI’s o1 model showed that when LLMs are trained to do the same—by using more compute during inference—they get significantly better at solving reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logic.

However, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret. That is, until last week, when DeepSeek released their DeepSeek-R1 model and promptly broke the internet (and the stock market!).

Besides performing as well or better than o1, the DeepSeek-R1 release was accompanied by a detailed tech report that outlined the key steps of their training recipe. This recipe involved several innovations, most notably the application of pure reinforcement learning to teach a base language model how to reason without any human supervision. As shown in the figure below, making a powerful reasoning model is now very simple if you have access to a capable base model and a high-quality data mixture:

However, the DeepSeek-R1 release leaves open several questions about:

These questions prompted us to launch the Open-R1 project, an initiative to systematically reconstruct DeepSeek-R1’s data and training pipeline, validate its claims, and push the boundaries of open reasoning models. By building Open-R1, we aim to provide transparency on how reinforcement learning can enhance reasoning, share reproducible insights with the open-source community, and create a foundation for future models to leverage these techniques.

In this blog post we take a look at key ingredients behind DeepSeek-R1, which parts we plan to replicate, and how to contribute to the Open-R1 project.

DeepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model built on the foundation of DeepSeek-V3. Like any good reasoning model, it starts with a strong base model, and DeepSeek-V3 is exactly that. This 671B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model performs on par with heavyweights like Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o. What’s especially impressive is how cost-efficient it was to train—just $5.5M—thanks to architectural changes like Multi Token Prediction (MTP), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and a LOT (seriously, a lot) of hardware optimization.

DeepSeek also introduced two models: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1, each with a distinct training approach. DeepSeek-R1-Zero skipped supervised fine-tuning altogether and relied entirely on reinforcement learning (RL), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to make the process more efficient. A simple reward system was used to guide the model, providing feedback based on the accuracy and structure of its answers. This approach helped the model develop useful reasoning skills, such as breaking problems into steps and verifying its own outputs. However, its responses often lacked clarity and were difficult to read.

That’s where DeepSeek-R1 comes in. It started with a "cold start" phase, fine-tuning on a small set of carefully crafted examples to improve clarity and readability. From there, it went through more RL and refinement steps, including rejecting low-quality outputs with both human preference based and verifiable reward, to create a model that not only reasons well but also produces polished and consistent answers.

This all sounds great, but what's actually missing? Let's have a look at the missing pieces of the puzzle.

The release of DeepSeek-R1 is an amazing boon for the community, but they didn’t release everything—although the model weights are open, the datasets and code used to train the model are not 😢.

The goal of Open-R1 is to build these last missing pieces so that the whole research and industry community can build similar or better models using these recipes and datasets. And by doing this in the open, everybody in the community can contribute!

As shown in the figure below, here’s our plan of attack:

Note that we don’t want to stop at math datasets. There’s a lot of potential in exploring other areas, obvious one like code but also scientific fields such as medicine, where reasoning models could have significant impact.

This initiative isn’t just about replicating results—it’s about sharing insights with the community. By documenting what works, what doesn’t, and why, we hope to save others from wasting time and compute on unproductive paths.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face, there are plenty of ways to get involved. Let’s build this together! 🚀

#10889. How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

Motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells users where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

It directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a new user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a new view slides in from the right, a short transition shows users where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, users repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help new users reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: users settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

Animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets users grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

The right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:

CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

The Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

Lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm users. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

For performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:

Beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

Motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your new users and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

The best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where users most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.

#10888. Welcome to Inference Providers on the Hub 🔥

Today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages. They are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for JS and Python), making it easier than ever to explore serverless inference of a wide variety of models that run on your favorite providers.

We’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we launched the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯). While this has enabled easy exploration and prototyping, we’ve refined our core value proposition towards collaboration, storage, versioning, and distribution of large datasets and models with the community. At the same time, serverless providers have flourished, and the time was right for Hugging Face to offer easy and unified access to serverless inference through a set of great providers.

Just as we work with great partners like AWS, Nvidia and others for dedicated deployment options via the model pages’ Deploy button, it was natural to partner with the next generation of serverless inference providers for model-centric, serverless inference.

Here’s what this enables, taking the timely example of DeepSeek-ai/DeepSeek-R1, a model which has achieved mainstream fame over the past few days 🔥:

Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder & CEO at SambaNova: "We are excited to be partnering with Hugging Face to accelerate its Inference API. Hugging Face developers now have access to much faster inference speeds on a wide range of the best open source models."

Zeke Sikelianos, Founding Designer at Replicate: "Hugging Face is the de facto home of open-source model weights, and has been a key player in making AI more accessible to the world. We use Hugging Face internally at Replicate as our weights registry of choice, and we're honored to be among the first inference providers to be featured in this launch."

This is just the start, and we’ll build on top of this with the community in the coming weeks!

The following example shows how to use DeepSeek-R1 using Together AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Together AI API key if you have one.

Install huggingface_hub version v0.28.0 or later (release notes).

Note: You can also use the OpenAI client library to call the Inference Providers too; see here an example for DeepSeek model.

And here's how to generate an image from a text prompt using FLUX.1-dev running on fal.ai:

To move to a different provider, you can simply change the provider name, everything else stays the same:

We expose the Routing proxy directly under the huggingface.co domain so you can call it directly, it's very useful for OpenAI-compatible APIs for instance. You can just swap the URL as a base URL: https://router.huggingface.co/{:provider}.

Here's how you can call Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct using Sambanova as the inference provider via cURL.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Together AI key you're billed on your Together AI account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Here’s a Hub discussion you can use: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49

This turn might not seem like that big of a deal to many of you... But in practice, this very clearly constitutes an abrupt cutting-off of the lion's share of the quasi-subsidized compute erstwhile accessible through HF.

And though seldom overtly publicized as a core feature of the platform, that nonchalantly encouraging compute reservoir of yore (even if accessible only via select pockets, like Inference Endpoints) served for years as a kind of a phantom fertilizer, and a key one, for Machine Learning adoption, experimentation, and resource-strapped development – on par with other quasi-subsidized resources like Google Colab and ChatGPT . And it's entirely plausible that the availability of such resources en masse has been the single most important prerequisite, as well as mandatory catalyst, for the continual evolution/democratization of open source ML specifically, whether in regards to utility or literacy or safety or any other oft-evoked marker, and in some large part the popularization of ML more broadly.

Of course, despite its qualitative obviousness, the impact of subsidized resources may be difficult, maybe impossible, to summate objectively or to quantify directly. After all they constitute a set of infrastructures the immediate production of which tends to assume forms that are often ephemeral, social – like practices, understanding, or values – and wherever concrete, often non-commercial, like open models, adapters, enthusiast contributions, articles, posts, etc. And by the markers of finance and markets, such productions may be deemed as having only a tangential value to, say, the capitalization potential of a given platform, all-the-while adding heavy and at times unforeseeably fluctuating costs upkeep.

Nonetheless, (and there are few better illustrations for this than ML) public access to subsidized resources persisting in open forms (non-transactional, nor overtly monetized, nor strictly delimited: like all public resources, services, libraries, spaces) simultaneously remains a key precondition for the economic and socio-cultural potential of the entire technological and research field as a whole, whilst continually stimulating the range and variety of forms this potential may ultimately assume.

As recently as a year ago, I would avidly preach the merits of Huggingface to everyone I know: not only as the key extant firmament for humanist and democratized machine learning paradigms to emerge and thrive upon, but as a really-existing pre-figuration of a new form of society, one that may at last transcend the intertwined logic of alienation, separation, disparity, scarcity, disposability, amnesia, exploitation, and all the rest of it... That's what I used to associate with Huggingface. Nowadays though: I think of Huggingface, and my next thought is "$2.00".

I know that for resources or platforms to remain subsidized, such subsidies must come from someplace. And assuring reliable funding may be a challenge, especially these days. Nonetheless, I really believe that it would be a grave mistake long-term for HF to rely on standard transactional/commercial monetization sourced from its users, even to cover real costs (much less to extract surplus "value" from or for anyone). To best serve its role within the field, HF must instead move closer to operating as a non-profit, sourcing unconditional funding from elsewhere , with the assumption that it may always operate at a "loss", whilst playing a key role in the thriving and the dynamism of the field as a whole.

#10887. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10886. How to deploy and fine-tune DeepSeek models on AWS

A running document to showcase how to deploy and fine-tune DeepSeek R1 models with Hugging Face on AWS.

If you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully. OpenAI’s o1 model showed that when LLMs are trained to do the same—by using more compute during inference—they get significantly better at solving reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logic.

However, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret. That is, until last week, when DeepSeek released their DeepSeek-R1 model and promptly broke the internet (and the stock market!).

DeepSeek AI open-sourced DeepSeek-R1-Zero, DeepSeek-R1, and six dense models distilled from DeepSeek-R1 based on Llama and Qwen architectures. You can find them all in the DeepSeek R1 collection.

We collaborate with Amazon Web Services to make it easier for developers to deploy the latest Hugging Face models on AWS services to build better generative AI applications.

Let’s review how you can deploy and fine-tune DeepSeek R1 models with Hugging Face on AWS.

Hugging Face Inference Endpoints offers an easy and secure way to deploy Machine Learning models on dedicated compute for use in production on AWS. Inference Endpoints empower developers and data scientists alike to create AI applications without managing infrastructure: simplifying the deployment process to a few clicks, including handling large volumes of requests with autoscaling, reducing infrastructure costs with scale-to-zero, and offering advanced security.

With Inference Endpoints, you can deploy any of the 6 distilled models from DeepSeek-R1 and also a quantized version of DeepSeek R1 made by Unsloth: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-GGUF. On the model page, click on Deploy, then on HF Inference Endpoints. You will be redirected to the Inference Endpoint page, where we selected for you an optimized inference container, and the recommended hardware to run the model. Once you created your endpoint, you can send your queries to DeepSeek R1 for 8.3$ per hour with AWS 🤯.

You can find DeepSeek R1 and distilled models, as well as other popular open LLMs, ready to deploy on optimized configurations in the Inference Endpoints Model Catalog.

#10885. The AI tools for Art Newsletter - Issue 1

The AI space is moving so fast it’s hard to believe that a year ago we still struggled to generate people with the correct amount of fingers 😂.

The last couple of years have been pivotal for open source models and tools for artistic usage. AI tools for creative expression have never been more accessible, and we’re only scratching the surface. Join us as we look back at the key milestones, tools, and breakthroughs in AI & Arts from 2024, and forward for what’s to come in 2025 (spoiler 👀: we’re starting a new monthly roundup 👇).

What were the standout releases of creative AI tools in 2024? We'll highlight the major releases across creative and artistic fields, with a particular focus on open-source developments in popular tasks like image and video generation.

Over 2 years since the OG stable diffusion was released and made waves in image generation with open source models, it’s now safe to say that when it comes to image generation from text, image editing and controlled image generation - open source models are giving closed source models a run for their money.

TD;LR - diffusion models and Gaussian flow matching are equivalent. Flow matching proposes a vector field parametrization of the network output that is different compared to the ones commonly used in diffusion models previously.

Back to practice: First to announce the shift was Stability AI with Stable Diffusion 3, however it was HunyuanDiT that became the first open source model with DiT architecture.This trend continued with the releases of AuraFlow, Flux.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5.

Among many pivotal moments in the (not so long) history of open source image generation models, it’s safe to say that the release of Flux.1 was one of them. Flux [dev] achieved a new state-of-the-art, surpassing popular closed source models like Midjourney v6.0, DALL·E 3 (HD) on various benchmarks.

A positive side effect of advancements in image models is the significant improvement in personalization techniques for text-to-image models and controlled generation.

Back in August 2022, transformative works like Textual Inversion and DreamBooth enhanced our ability to teach and introduce new concepts to text-to-image models, drastically expanding what could be done with them. These opened the door to a stream of improvements and enhancements building on top of these techniques (such as LoRA for diffusion models).

However, an upper bound to the quality of the fine-tuned models is naturally the base model from which it was fine-tuned. In that sense, we can’t neglect Stable Diffusion XL, which was also a significant marker in personalization for open source image generation models. A testimony to that is that even now, many of the popular techniques and models for personalization and controlled generation are based on SDXL. The advanced abilities of SDXL (and models that were released after with similar quality) together with the growing understanding of the semantic roles of different components in the diffusion model architecture raises the question - what can we achieve without further optimization?

cue in the rain of zero shot techniques - 2024 was definitely the year when generating high quality portraits from reference photos was made possible with as little as a single reference image & without any optimization. Training free techniques like IP adapter FaceID, InstantID, Photomaker and more came out and demonstrated competitive if not even superior abilities to those of fine-tuned models.

Similarly, image editing and controlled generation - such as image generation with canny / depth / pose constraints made progress too - both thanks to the growing quality of the base models and the community’s growing understanding of the semantic roles different components have (Instant Style, B-LoRA)

So what’s next? since the shift of paradigms to DiT and flow matching objectives, additional models came out trying to utilize DiT-based models like Flux and SD3.5 for similar purposes, but so far not quite beating the quality of the SDXL-based ones despite the superior quality of the underlying base model. This could be attributed to the relative lack of understanding of semantic roles of different components of the DiT compared to the Unet. 2025 could be the year when we identify those roles in DiTs as well, unlocking more possibilities with the next generation of image generation models.

As opposed to image generation, with video we still have a way to go. But, it’s safe to say that we’re very far away from where we were a year ago. While we’re all about open-source, the credit for (some) of the significant leap in AI video generation goes to OpenAI’s sora for changing our expectations of video model capabilities quite radically. And as fofr put nicely in AI video is having its Stable Diffusion moment (which we recommend reading 🙂) - it made everyone realize what is possible.

The recent surge of open-source video generation models, including CogVideoX, Mochi, Allegro, LTX Video, and HunyuanVideo, has also been noteworthy. Video generation is inherently more challenging than image generation due to the need for motion quality, coherence, and consistency. Additionally, video generation requires substantial computational and memory resources, leading to significant generation latency. This often hinders local usage, making many new open video models inaccessible to community hardware without extensive memory optimizations and quantization approaches that impact both inference latency and the quality of generated videos. Nevertheless the open source community has made remarkable progress - which was recently covered in this blog on the state of open video generation models.

While this implies that most community members are still unable to experiment and develop with open-source video models, it also suggests that we can expect significant advancements in 2025.

Audio generation has progressed significantly in the past year going from simple sounds to complete songs with lyrics. Despite challenges - Audio signals are complex and multifaceted, require more sophisticated mathematical models than models that generate text or images and training data quite scarce - 2024 saw open source releases like OuteTTS and IndicParlerTTS for text to speech and openai’s Whisper large v3 turbo for audio speech recognition. The year 2025 is already shaping up to be a breakthrough year for audio models, with a remarkable number of releases in January alone. We've seen the release of three new text-to-speech models: Kokoro, LLasa TTS and OuteTTS 0.3, as well as two new music models: JASCO and YuE. With this pace, we can expect even more exciting developments in the audio space throughout the year.

The beauty of open source is that it allows the community to experiment, find new usages for existing models / pipelines, improve on and build new tools together. Many of the creative AI tools that were popular this year are the fruit of joint community effort.

Many of the amazing Flux fine-tunes created in the last year were trained thanks to the AI-toolkit by ostris.

Inspired by fofr's face-to-many, Face to All combines the viral Instant ID model with added ControlNet depth constraints and community fine-tuned SDXL LoRAs to create training-free and high-quality portraits in creative stylizations.

Based on a ComfyUI workflow by Nathan Shipley, Flux style shaping combines Flux [dev] Redux and Flux [dev] Depth for style transfer and optical illusion creation.

Diffusers Image Outpaint makes use of the diffusers Stable Diffusion XL Fill Pipeline together with an SDXL union controlnet to seamlessly expand an input image.

Adding mimics to a static portrait was never easier with Live Portrait and Face Poke.

TRELLIS is a 3D generation model for versatile and high-quality 3D asset creation that took over the 3D landscape with a bang.

IC-Light, which stands for "Imposing Consistent Light", is a tool for relighting with foreground condition.

2025 is the year for open-source to catch up on video, movement, and audio models, making room for more modalities. With advancements in efficient computing and quantization, we can expect significant leaps in open-source video models. As we approach a (natural) plateau in image generation models, we can shift our focus to other tasks and modalities.

YuE - series of open-source music foundation models for full song generation. YuE is possibly the best open source model for music generation (with an Apache 2.0 license!), achieving competitive results to closed source models like Suno.

try it out & read more: demo, model weights.

Hunyuan 3D-2 , SPAR3D, DiffSplat - 3D generation models. 3D models are coming in hot - not long after the release of TRELLIS, Hunyuan 3D-2, SPAR3D and DiffSplat are here to take over the 3D landscape.

Lumina-Image 2.0 - text to image model. Lumina is a 2B parameter model competitive with the 12B Flux.1 [dev] and with an Apache 2.0 license(!!).

try it out & read more: demo, model weights.

ComfyUI-to-Gradio - a step-by-step guide on how to convert a complex ComfyUI workflow to a simple Gradio application, and how to deploy this application on Hugging Face Spaces ZeroGPU serverless structure, which allows for it to be deployed and run for free in a serverless manner read more here.

Kicking off with this blog, we (Poli & Linoy) will be bringing you a monthly roundup of the latest in the creative AI world. In such a fast-evolving space, it’s tough to stay on top of all the new developments, let alone sift through them. That’s where we come in & hopefully this way we can make creative AI tools more accessible

#10884. How to Use CSS Attribute Selectors to Build More Flexible User Interfaces

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10883. Mini-R1: Reproduce Deepseek R1 „aha moment“ a RL tutorial

This post was written by Philipp Schmid and orginially posted on philschmid.de code can found here.

The release of Deepseek R1 shocked the industry. Why? Well, DeepSeek-R1 is an open model that rivals OpenAI's o1 in complex reasoning tasks, introduced using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and RL-focused multi-stage training approach. They not only released the model, but also a research paper on how they did it.

In the paper they described an "aha moment" when using pure RL to train the model. During this phase, DeepSeek-R1-Zero (the first test of DeepSeek-R1) learns to allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach without any human feedback or data describing how to do it. They describe this as an "aha moment" as:

This behavior is not only a testament to the model’s growing reasoning abilities but also a captivating example of how reinforcement learning can lead to unexpected and sophisticated outcomes.

In this blog post we want to recreate the small "aha moment" of DeepSeek-R1 using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and the Countdown Game. We will train an open model using reinforcement learning trying to teach it self-verification and search abilities all on its own to solve the Countdown Game. The Countdown game is a numbers puzzle where players use a set of randomly drawn numbers and basic arithmetic operations (+, -, ×, ÷) to reach or get as close as possible to a target number.

The blog post focuses on training distributed training using Deepspeed and vLLM. It was run on a 4x NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Note: This blog is inspired by Jiayi Pan who initially explored the idea and proofed it with a small model.

But Before we start, let's take a look at the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and understand how it works.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm to improve the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. It was introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper in the context of mathematical reasoning. GRPO modifies the traditional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) by eliminating the need for a value function model. Instead, it estimates baselines from group scores, reducing memory usage and computational overhead. GRPO, now also used by the Qwen team, can be used with rule/binary-based Rewards as well as General Reward Models to improve models on helpfulness.

Our first step is to install Hugging Face Libraries and Pytorch, vllm, and trl, transformers and datasets. If you haven't heard of trl yet, don't worry. It is a new library on top of transformers and datasets, which makes it easier to fine-tune, rlhf, align open LLMs.

Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.

We will use the Hugging Face Hub as a remote model versioning service. This means we will automatically push our model, logs and information to the Hub during training. You must register on the Hugging Face for this. After you have an account, we will use the login util from the huggingface_hub package to log into our account and store our token (access key) on the disk.

We are going to use the Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4 dataset, which contains samples with 3 to 4 numbers and solutions. As Model we are going to use Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct which is a 3B parameter instruction tuned model. This makes it easier to showcase the "aha moment" as it already can follow instructions. Jiayi-Pan explored that the model needs to have a certain quality to be able to learn the reasoning process, starting with > 1.5B parameters.

TRL supports Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) through a dedicated GRPOTrainer for aligning LLMs from preference data, as described in DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. The GRPOTrainer is a subclass of the Trainer from the transformers library and supports all the same features, including logging, checkpointing, distributed training, and parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

The GRPOTrainer supports generic Outcome Reward Models (ORM) and custom reward functions, that can be used to implement Rule-Based Reward Models. In the Deepseek R1 paper they implemented Rule-Based Reward Models to verify the correctness of the generated solutions. In our exmaple we are going to do a similar approach, where we will create 2 reward functions that:

Note: Correct in our example includes the equation, for example 55 + 36 - 7 - 19

Hugging Face TRL added support for distributed training with Deepspeed and using vLLM for faster generation. I preprared a run_r1_grpo.py script and a receipes/grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file to run the training.

This configuration is tested and validated on a Node with 4x H100 80GBs, where a single step takes around 45-60s, as we can leverage vLLM for generation and DeepSpeed for distributed training. Therefore we need to make sure we correctly set the num_processes to the number of GPUs you have - 1 as the last one will be used with vLLM for Generation. If you are using more GPUS you need to change the vllm_device in the config file to last index GPU, e.g. if you have 8 GPUs you need to set vllm_device=7 and your num_processes to 7.

With the optimized distributed training a single step with 8 generations per sample on 4x H100 80GBs takes around 45-60s. The full training for 450 steps takes around 6 hours.

The script saves random completions to the completion_samples folder, which you can use to inspect the model's progress. It includes completion_samples.txt and success_completion_samples.txt. The completion_samples.txt includes all completions, while the success_completion_samples.txt which correctly solves the equation. Below you can find the interesating training obeserations on how the performance changes over time, as well as the Tensornoard logs and successfull reasoning samples.

The model with checkpoints for every 25th step can be found at philschmid/qwen-2.5-3b-r1-countdown.

I started the experiment using the hyperparameters from the DeepSeekMath paper with a learning rate of 1e-6 and a beta (KL coefficient) of 0.04, which led to unstable training runs after around 150 steps. I ran some small ablations and decreased both the learning rate to 5e-7 and the beta to 0.001, based on a test from OpenRLHF. I coulnd't test how increasing the num_generations from 8 to 64 would affect the training. 64 is the generation value, which was used in the DeepSeekMath paper. All other parameters can be found in the grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file.

I have 3 potential assumptions why the model shifts from "word reasoning" to "programmatic execution":

The release of DeepSeek R1 and its research paper might be a breakpoint for open-science and open-source development. Just a week after the DeepSeek release, we've been able to reproduce a simple version of R1 learned "reasoning" using GRPO and the Countdown Game. While our implementation focuses on a specific task rather than general reasoning and convergence into a very specific "reasoning" format, it shows that the method is working.

Looking in to 2025, it's clear that we are on the cusp of even more significant progress. RL will become more accessible and user-friendly, more researchers and developers will explore its potential, but also require amount of more compute as before and compared to supervised fine-tuning.

I am excited for 2025. If you have any questions or ideas, feel free to reach out to me.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face.

#10882. Open-R1: Update #1

It’s been two weeks since the release of DeepSeek R1 and just a week since we started the open-r1 project to replicate the missing pieces, namely the training pipeline and the synthetic data. This post summarizes:

It should serve both as an update on the project and as a collection of interesting resources around DeepSeek-R1.

Let’s start by looking at the progress we made on Open-R1. We started Open-R1 just one week ago and people across the teams as well as the community came together to work on it and we have some progress to report.

The first step in reproduction is to verify that we can match the evaluation scores. We are able to reproduce Deepseek's reported results on the MATH-500 Benchmark:

You can find the instructions to run these evaluations in the open-r1 repository.

One observation we have made is the enormous size of the generations from the DeepSeek models, which makes even evaluating the model challenging. Here we show DeepSeek-R1 response lengths in the OpenThoughts dataset:

Distribution of R1’s responses shows that they are on average very long with the average response being 6,000 tokens long and some responses containing more than 20,000 tokens. Worth noting that the average page contains ~500 words and one token is on average slightly less than a word, which means the many reponses are over 10 pages long. (src: https://x.com/gui_penedo/status/1884953463051649052)

The length of responses will make GPRO training challenging, as we will have to generate long completions which will require a significant proportion of GPU memory to store the activations / gradients for the optimization step.

In order to share our progress publicly, we have created an open-r1 evaluation leaderboard, so the community can follow our reproduction efforts (space is here):

Following the release of Open R1, GRPO (Grouped Relative Policy Optimization) was integrated into the latest TRL release (version 0.14). This integration enables training any model with one or multiple reward functions or models. The GRPO implementation integrates with DeepSpeed ZeRO 1/2/3 for parallelized training that scales to many GPUs, and uses vLLM for fast generation, which is the primary bottleneck in online training methods.

There are still some limitations relating to the use of high memory usage, and progress is being made to profile and reduce them.

One of the most exciting findings of the R1 report was that the main model can be used to generate synthetic reasoning traces and smaller models fine-tuned on this dataset see similar performance gains as the main model. So naturally we want to re-create the synthetic reasoning dataset as well such that the community can fine-tune other models on it.

With a model as big as R1 the main challenge is scaling up generation efficiently and fast. We spent a week tinkering with various setups and configurations.

The model fits on two 8xH100 nodes so naturally we started experimenting with that setup and used vLLM as inference server. However, we quickly noticed that this configuration is not ideal: the throughput is sub-optimal and only allows for 8 parallel request, because the GPU KV cache fills up too quickly. What happens when the cache fills up ist that the requests which use a lot of cache are preempted and if the config uses PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE the requests are scheduled again later when more VRAM is available.

We then switched to a setup with 4x 8xH100 nodes, so 32 GPUs in total. This leaves enough spare VRAM for 32 requests running in parallel with barely any of them getting rescheduled due to 100% cache utilization.

Originally we started querying the vLLM servers with batches of requests but noticed quickly, that straggles in the batches would cause the GPU utiliziation to vary since a new batch would only start processing once the last sample of the previous batch is done. Switching the batched inference to streaming helped stabilize the GPU utilization significantly:

It only required changing the code sending requests to the vLLM servers. The code for batched inference:

We are generating at a fairly constant rate but might still explore a bit further if for example switching to the CPU cache is a better strategy when long queries get preempted.

The current inference code can be found here.

There has been wide interest in open-r1, including from the media so various team members have been in the news in the past week:

Other mentions: Washington Post, Financial Times, Financial Times, Fortune, Fortune, The Verge, Financial Review, Tech Crunch, Die Zeit, Financial Times, New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, EuroNews, Barrons, New York Times, Vox, Nature, SwissInfo, Handelsblatt, Business Insider, IEEE Spectrum, MIT Tech Review, LeMonde.

While the community is still digesting DeepSeek-R1’s results and report, DeepSeek has captured broader public attention just two weeks after its release.

After a relatively calm first week post-release, the second week saw significant market reactions, prompting responses from multiple AI research labs:

In parallel, several companies worked on providing the DeepSeek models through various platforms (non-exhaustive list):

There has been a lot of interest around the proclaimed cost of training V3/R1. While the exact number probably doesn’t matter so much, people worked on some back-of-the-envelope calculations to verify the order of magnitude here. TL;DR the numbers seem generally in the right order of magnitude, as seen in these discussions:

As many groups are working on reproducing the training pipeline, we’ll get more evidence on the possible training efficiency for the model.

Last week some speculations surfaced that DeepSeek might have been using OpenAI outputs to train its models. See for example the Financial Times. However, it is unclear at this point what the consequences of these allegations will be.

The open source community has been extremely active around DeepSeek-R1 and many people started building interesting projects around the model.

There have been a number of projects that try to reproduce the basic learning mechanics at smaller scale, so you can test the basic learning principles at home.

The community has been busy on a number of dataset efforts related to R1, some highlights include:

This list only covers a small number of reasoning and problem solving related datasets on the Hub. We’re excited to see what other datasets the community build in the coming weeks.

We are just getting started and want to finish the training pipeline and try it on smaller models and use the scaled up inference pipeline to generate high quality datasets. If you want to contribute check out the open-r1 repository on GitHub or follow the Hugging Face open-r1 org.
