#10873. Build awesome datasets for video generation

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak)

Tooling for image generation datasets is well established, with img2dataset being a fundamental tool used for large scale dataset preparation, and complemented with various community guides, scripts and UIs that cover smaller scale initiatives.

Our ambition is to make tooling for video generation datasets equally established, by creating open video dataset scripts suited for small scale, and leveraging video2dataset for large scale use cases.

“If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants”

In this post, we provide an overview of the tooling we are developing to make it easy for the community to build their own datasets for fine-tuning video generation models. If you cannot wait to get started already, we welcome you to check out the codebase here.

Typically, video generation is conditioned on natural language text prompts such as: "A cat walks on the grass, realistic style". Then in a video, there are a number of qualitative aspects for controllability and filtering, like so:

Video generation models are only as good as the data they are trained on. Therefore, these aspects become crucial when curating the datasets for training/fine-tuning.

Our 3 stage pipeline draws inspiration from works like Stable Video Diffusion, LTX-Video, and their data pipelines.

Like video2dataset we opt to use yt-dlp for downloading videos.

We create a script Video to Scenes to split long videos into short clips.

Florence-2 microsoft/Florence-2-large to run Florence-2 tasks , , and on extracted frames. This provides different captions, object recognition and OCR that can be used for filtering in various ways.

We can bring in any other captioner in this regard. We can also caption the entire video (e.g., with a model like Qwen2.5) as opposed to captioning individual frames.

In the dataset for the model finetrainers/crush-smol-v0, we opted for captions from Qwen2VL and we filtered on pwatermark < 0.1 and aesthetic > 5.5. This highly restrictive filtering resulted in 47 videos out of 1493 total.

Let's review the example frames from pwatermark -

Two with text have scores of 0.69 and 0.61

The "toy car with a bunch of mice in it" scores 0.60 then 0.17 as the toy car is crushed.

All example frames were filtered by pwatermark < 0.1. pwatermark is effective at detecting text/watermarks however the score gives no indication whether it is a text overlay or a toy car's license plate. Our filtering required all scores to be below the threshold, an average across frames would be a more effective strategy for pwatermark with a threshold of around 0.2 - 0.3.

Let's review the example frames from aesthetic scores -

The pink castle initially scores 5.5 then 4.44 as it is crushed

The action figure scores lower at 4.99 dropping to 4.84 as it is crushed.

In our filtering we required all scores to be below the threshold, in this case using the aesthetic score from the first frame only would be a more effective strategy.

If we review finetrainers/crush-smol we can notice that many of the objects being crushed are round or rectangular and colorful which is similar to our findings in the example frames. Aesthetic scores can be useful yet have a bias that will potentially filter out good data when used with extreme thresholds like > 5.5. It may be more effective as a filter for bad content than good with a minimum threshold of around 4.25 - 4.5.

Here we provide some visual examples for each filter as well as the captions from Florence-2.

We have created various datasets with the tooling in an attempt to generate cool video effects, similar to the Pika Effects:

We then used these datasets to fine-tune the CogVideoX-5B model using finetrainers. Below is an example output from finetrainers/crush-smol-v0:

We hope this tooling gives you a headstart to create small and high-quality video datasets for your own custom applications. We will continue to add more useful filters to the repository, so, please keep an eye out. Your contributions are also more than welcome 🤗

#10872. From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository. The idea is straightforward: break each file’s data into chunks, store only unique ones, reap the benefits.

In practice, it's more complex. If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size. By doing that, we’d create significant overheads for the infrastructure and the builders on the Hub.

On Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases). Our guiding principle is simple: enable rapid experimentation and collaboration for teams building and iterating on models and datasets. This means focusing on more than just deduplication; we’re optimizing how data moves across the network, how it’s stored, and the entire development experience.

Imagine uploading a 200GB repository to the Hub. Today, there are a number of ways to do this, but all use a file-centric approach. To bring faster file transfers to the Hub, we've open-sourced xet-core and hf_xet, an integration with huggingface_hub which uses a chunk-based approach written in Rust.

If you consider a 200GB repository with unique chunks, that's 3 million entries (at ~64KB per chunk) in the content-addressed store (CAS) backing all repositories. If a new version of a model is uploaded or a branch in the repository is created with different data, more unique chunks are added, driving up the entries in the CAS.

With nearly 45PB across 2 million model, dataset, and space repositories on the Hub, a purely chunk-based approach could incur 690 billion chunks. Managing this volume of content using only chunks is simply not viable due to:

In short, network requests balloon, databases struggle to manage the metadata, and the cost of orchestrating each chunk skyrockets all while you wait for your files to transfer.

These challenges lead to a key realization:

Deduplication is a performance optimization, not the final goal.

The final goal is to improve the experience of builders iterating and collaborating on models and datasets. The system components from the client to the storage layer do not need to guarantee deduplication. Instead, they leverage deduplication as one tool among many to aid in this.

By loosening the deduplication constraint, we naturally arrive at a second design principle:

Avoid communication or storage strategies that scale 1:1 with the number of chunks.

What does this mean? We scale with aggregation.

Aggregation takes chunks and groups them, referencing them intelligently in ways that provide clever (and practical) benefits:

Together, blocks and shards unlock significant benefits. However, when someone uploads a new file, how do we know if a chunk has been uploaded before so we can eliminate an unnecessary request? Performing a network query for every chunk is not scalable and goes against the “no 1:1” principle we mentioned above.

The solution is key chunks which are a 0.1% subset of all chunks selected with a simple modulo condition based on the chunk hash. We provide a global index over these key chunks and the shards they are found in, so that when the chunk is queried, the related shard is returned to provide local deduplication. This allows us to leverage the principles of spatial locality. If a key chunk is referenced in a shard, it’s likely that other similar chunk references are available in the same shard. This further improves deduplication and reduces network and database requests.

The Hub currently stores over 3.5PB of .gguf files, most of which are quantized versions of other models on the Hub. Quantized models represent an interesting opportunity for deduplication due to the nature of quantization where values are restricted to a smaller integer range and scaled. This restricts the range of values in the weight matrices, naturally leading to more repetition. Additionally, many repositories of quantized models store multiple different variants (e.g., Q4_K, Q3_K, Q5_K) with a great deal of overlap.

A good example of this in practice is bartowski/gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF which contains 29 quantizations of google/gemma-2-9b-it totalling 191GB. To upload, we use hf_xet integrated with huggingface_hub to perform chunk-level deduplication locally then aggregate and store data at the block level.

Once uploaded, we can start to see some cool patterns! We’ve included a visualization that shows the deduplication ratio for each block. The darker the block, the more frequently parts of it are referenced across model versions. If you go to the Space hosting this visualization, hovering over any heatmap cell highlights all references to the block in orange across all models while clicking on a cell will select all other files that share blocks:

A single block of deduplication might only represent a few MB of savings, but as you can see there are many overlapping blocks! With this many blocks that quickly adds up. Instead of uploading 191GB, the Xet-backed version of the gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF repository stores 1515 unique blocks for a total of approximately 97GB to our test CAS environment (a savings of ~94GB).

While the storage improvements are significant, the real benefit is what this means for contributors to the Hub. At 50MB/s, the deduplication optimizations amount to a four hour difference in upload time; a speedup of nearly 2x:

Similarly, local chunk caching significantly speeds up downloads. If a file is changed or a new quantization is added that has significant overlap with the local chunk cache, you won’t have to re-download any chunks that are unchanged. This contrasts to the file-based approach where the entirety of the new or updated file must be downloaded.

Taken together, this demonstrates how local chunk-level deduplication paired with block-level aggregation dramatically streamlines not just storage, but developing on the Hub. By providing this level of efficiency in file transfers, AI builders can move faster, iterate quickly, and worry less about hitting infrastructure bottlenecks. For anyone pushing large files to the Hub (whether you're pushing a new model quantization or an updated version of a training set) this helps you shift focus to building and sharing, rather than waiting and troubleshooting.

We’re fast at work, rolling out the first Xet-backed repositories in the coming weeks and months! As we do that, we will be releasing more updates to bring these speeds to every builder on the Hub to make file transfers feel invisible.

Follow us on the Hub to learn more about our progress!

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash? The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash"?

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash?

Chunk hash is calculated via content-defined chunking (CDC), which means that if two chunks have the same content they will share the same hash. CDC removes the need to store the mapping between chunk hash -> chunk content because we know if two chunks share the same hash, they will have identical content.

The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

This is explained in the "key chunks" section in the blog post above. Essentially we only store a tiny subset of chunk -> block by leveraging spatial locality in the file. Trying to store every mapping of chunk -> block can get impractical very quickly.

what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash"

You can think of the shards as storing mappings between file (identified via file hash) to list of chunks that make up the file.

I hope this help explains our underlying tech better!

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file. For example if a model does not have a key chunk, the shard info only contains "file hash -> list of chunks", the CAS only has "block hash -> block content", how can we know which block is needed ?

For example if a model does not have a key chunk

Two points of clarification might be in order concerning the above point:

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file

When downloading a model file, a request is made to our services with the file hash. This is mapped to a list of block subranges. Logically these are chunks, but by storing the offsets we save on the metadata storage and ultimately many offsets will share boundaries inside a block (allowing us to group them together in a response) providing benefits when sending the content back to the client.

#10871. Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a new analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:

Revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

The two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed plan includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

List required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

PageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

The difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

Not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

No. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

Do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback plan—not just a favorable percentage.

#10870. 1 Billion Classifications

You’ve optimized your model. Your pipeline is running smoothly. But now, your cloud bill has skyrocketed. Running 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day isn’t just a technical challenge—it’s a financial one. How do you process at this scale without blowing your budget? Whether you're running large-scale document classification or bulk embedding pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), you need cost-efficient, high-throughput inference to make it feasible, and you get that from having a well optimized configuration.

These tasks often use encoder models, which are much smaller than modern LLMs, but at the 1B+ inference request scale it's still quite a non-trivial task. Just to be clear, that's English Wikipedia 144x over. I haven’t seen much information on how to approach this with cost in mind and I want to tackle that. This blog breaks down HOW to calculate cost and latency for large scale classification and embedding. We’ll analyze different model architectures, benchmark costs across hardware choices, and give you a clear framework for optimizing your own setup. Additionally we should be able to build some intuition if you don't feel like going through the process yourself.

Here is the code to make it happen: https://github.com/datavistics/encoder-analysis

tl;I'm not gonna reproduce this, tell me what you found;dr

With this pricing I was able to get this cost:

To evaluate cost and latency we need 4 key components:

I’ll be leveraging Inference Endpoints for my Hardware Options, as it allows me to choose from a wide range of hardware choices. Do note you can replace that with your GPUs of choice/consideration. For the Deployment Facilitator I'll be using the ever so useful Hugging Face Hub Library which allows me to programmatically deploy models easily.

For the Inference Server I’ll also be using Infinity which is an amazing library for serving encoder based models (and more now!). I’ve already written about TEI, which is another amazing library. You should definitely consider TEI when approaching your use-case, though this blog focuses on methodology rather than framework comparisons. Infinity has a number of key strengths, like serving multimodal embeddings, targeting different hardware (AMD, Nvidia, CPU and Inferentia) and running any new models that contain remote code that have not been integrated into huggingface’s transformer library. The most important of these to me is that most models are compatible by default.

For Load Testing I'll be using k6 from Grafana which is an open-source load testing tool written in go with a javascript interface. It’s easily configurable, has high performance, and has low overhead. It has a lot of built-in executors that are super useful. It also pre-allocates Virtual Users (VUs), which can be much more realistic than throwing some testing together yourself.

I'll go through 3 use-cases that should cover a variety of interesting points:

Optimization is a tricky issue, as there is a lot to consider. At a high level, I want to sweep across important load testing parameters and find what works best for a single GPU, as most encoder models will fit in a single GPU. Once we have a baseline of cost for a single GPU, the number of GPUs and throughput can be scaled horizontally by increasing the number of replica GPUs.

For each use-case this is the high-level flow I’ll use:

Since you have the code, feel free to adjust any part of this to your:

VUs and Batch Size are important because these influence how well we take advantage of all the compute available in the GPU. A large enough Batch Size makes sure we are fully utilizing the Streaming Multiprocessors and VRAM. There are scenarios where we have VRAM left over but there is a bandwidth cost that prevents throughput from increasing. So experimentation can help us. VUs allow us to make sure we are fully utilizing the batch size we have available.These are the main parameters I'll be testing:

Depending on your model you might want to consider:

K6 is great because it allows you to pre-allocate VUs and prevent some insidious bugs. It's quite flexible in how you are sending requests. I decided to use it in a specific way.

When I'm calling a k6 experiment, I mainly want to know what the throughput and average latency is for the requests, and have a few sanity checks for the load testing parameters I have chosen. I also want to do a sweep which means many experiments.

I use the shared-iterations executor (docs) which means K6 shares iterations between the number of VUs. The test ends once k6 executes all iterations. This allows me to have a reasonable time-out, but also put through enough requests to have a decent confidence that I can discriminate between load testing parameters choices in my sweep. In contrast to other executors, this allows me to be confident that I'm simulating the client working as hard as possible per VU which should show me what the cheapest option is.

I use 10_000 requests† and have a max experiment time of 1 min. So if 10_000 requests aren’t finished by 1 minute, then that experiment is over.

† I use less max requests for the Vision Embeddings given that the throughput is much lower and images are heavy.†† P95 means that 95% of requests complete within this time. It represents the worst-case latency for most users.

You can find the 3 notebooks that put the optimization workflow together here:

The main purpose was to get my experiments defined, launch the correct Inference Endpoint with the right parameters, and launch k6 with the right parameters to test the endpoint.

I made a couple design choices which you may want to think through to see if they work for you:

Text Classification can have a variety of use-cases at scale, like Email Filtering, Toxicity Detection in pre-training datasets, etc. The OG classic architecture was BERT, and quickly many other architectures came about. Do note that in contrast to popular decoder models, these need to be fine-tuned on your task before using them. Today I think the following architectures† are the most notable:

† Do note that for these models, you typically need to fine-tune this on your data to perform well†† I'm using “Engineering performance” to denote anticipated latency/throughput

I chose DistilBERT to focus on as it’s a great lightweight choice for many applications. I compared 2 GPUs, nvidia-t4 and nvidia-l4 as well as 2 Infinity Docker Images.

You can see the results in an interactive format here or in the space embedded below in the Analysis section. This is the cheapest configuration across the experiments I ran:

Text Embeddings are a loose way of describing the task of taking a text input and projecting it into a semantic space where close points are similar in meaning and distant ones are dissimilar (example below). This is used heavily in RAG and is an important part of AI search (which some are fans of).

There are a large number of architectures which are compatible, and you can see the most performant ones in the MTEB Leaderboard.

ModernBERT is the most exciting encoder release since DeBERTa back in 2020. It has all the ahem modern tricks built into an old and familiar architecture. It makes for an attractive model to experiment with as it's much less explored than other architectures and has a lot more potential. There are a number of improvements in speed and performance, but the most notable for a user is likely the 8k context window. Do check out this blog for a more thorough understanding.

It's important to note that Flash Attention 2 will only work with more modern GPUs due to the compute capability requirement, so I opted to skip the T4 in favor of the L4. An H100 would also work really well here for the heavy hitters category.

You can see the results in an interactive format here. This is the cheapest configuration across the experiments I ran:

ColQwen2 is a Visual Retriever which is based on the Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and uses ColBERT style multi-vector representations of both text and images. We can see that it has a complex architecture compared to the encoders we explored above.

There are a number of use-cases which might benefit from this at large scale like, e-commerce search, multi-modal recommendations, enterprise multi-modal RAG, etc

ColBERT style is different than our previous embedding use-case since it breaks the input into multiple tokens and returns a vector for each instead of 1 vector for the input. You can find an excellent tutorial from Jina AI here.This can lead to superior semantic encoding and better retrieval, but is also slower, and more expensive.

I'm excited for this experiment as it explores 2 lesser known concepts, vision embeddings and ColBERT style embeddings†. There are a few things to note about ColQwen2/VLMs:

†Do check out this more detailed blog if this is new and interesting to you.

I wanted to try a small and modern GPU like the nvidia-l4 since it should be able to fit the 2B param model but also scale well since it's cheap. Like the other embedding model, I'm varying batch_size and vus.

You can see the results in an interactive format here. This is the cheapest configuration across the experiments I ran:

Do check out the detailed analysis in this space (derek-thomas/classification-analysis) for the classification use-case (hide side-bar and scroll down for the charts):

Scaling to 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day is a non-trivial challenge, but with the right optimizations, it can be made cost-effective. From my experiments, a few key patterns emerged:

Your data, hardware, models, etc might differ, but I hope you find some use in the approach and code provided. The best way to get an estimate is to run this on your own task with your own configurations. Let's get exploring!

Special thanks to andrewrreed/auto-bench for some inspiration, Michael Feil for creating Infinity. Also thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Erik Kaunismaki, and Tom Aarsen for helping me review.

It's important to scale sanity checks as your complexity scales. Since we are using subprocess and jinja to then call k6 I felt far from the actual testing so I put a few checks in place.

The goal of task performance is that for a specific configuration we are performing similarly to what we expect. Task Performance will have different meanings across tasks. For classification I chose accuracy, and for embeddings I skipped it. We could look at average similarity and other similar metrics. It gets a bit more complex with ColBERT style since we are getting many vectors per request.

Even though 58% isn't bad for some 3 class classification tasks, it's irrelevant. The goal is to make sure that we are getting the expected task performance. If we see a significant change (increase or decrease) we should be suspicious and try to understand why.

Below is a great example from the classification use-case since we can see an extremely tight distribution and one outlier. Upon further investigation the outlier is due to a low amount of requests sent.

You can see the interactive results visualized by nbviewer here:

We should expect to see no failed requests as Inference Endpoints has a queue to handle extra requests. This is relevant for all 3 use-cases: Classification, Embedding, and Vision Embedding.

sum(df.total_requests - df.successful_requests) allows us to see if we had any failed requests.

As described above we are using a nice strategy of using exponential increases and then a binary search to find the best number of VUs. But how do we know that we tried enough VUs? What if we tried a higher amount of VUs and throughput kept increasing? If that's the case then we would see a monotonically increasing relationship between VUs and Throughput and we would need to run more tests.

You can see the interactive results visualized by nbviewer here:

When we request an embedding it makes sense that we would always get back an embedding of the same size as specified by the model type. You can see the checks here:

We are using a ColBERT style model for Vision Embedding which means we should be getting multiple vectors per image. It's interesting to see the distribution of these as it allows us to check for anything unexpected and to get to know our data. To do so I stored the min_num_vectors, avg_num_vectors, max_num_vectors, in the experiments.

We should expect to see some variance in all 3, but it’s ok that min_num_vectors and max_num_vectors have the same value across experiments.

Here is a short description, but you can get a more detailed interactive experience in the space: derek-thomas/classification-analysis

For the classification use-case we looked at 2 different Infinity Images, default and trt-onnx. Which one was better? It's best if we can compare these across the same settings (GPU, batch_size, VUs). We can simply group our results by those settings and then see which one was cheaper.

This is a key chart as for many use-cases there is a maximum latency that a user can experience. Usually if we allow the latency to increase we can increase throughput creating a trade-off scenario. That's true in all the use-cases I've looked at here. Having a pareto curve is great to help visualize where that tradeoff is.

Lastly it's important to build intuition on what is happening when we try these different settings. Do we get beautiful idealized charts? Do we see unexpected gradients? Do we need more exploration in a region? Could we have issues in our setup like not having an isolated environment? All of these are good questions and some can be tricky to answer.

The contour plot is built by interpolating intermediate points in a space defined by the 3 dimensions. There are a couple phenomena that are worth understanding:

We can see a complex contour chart with some interesting results from the classification use-case:

But here is a much cleaner one from the vision-embedding task:

For actual usage, do consider using the infinity client. When we are benchmarking it's good practice to use k6 to know what’s possible. For actual usage, use the official lib, or something close for a few benefits:

You also have OpenAI lib compatibility with the Infinity backend as another option.

#10869. Fixing Open LLM Leaderboard with Math-Verify

3 weeks ago, we showed how hard it is to correctly evaluate LLM performance on math problems, and introduced Math-Verify, a better solution to validate models on math (read more in the announcement)!

Today, we’re thrilled to share that we’ve used Math-Verify to thoroughly re-evaluate all 3,751 models ever submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard, for even fairer and more robust model comparisons!

The Open LLM Leaderboard is the most used leaderboard on the Hugging Face Hub: it compares open Large Language Models (LLM) performance across various tasks. One of these tasks, called MATH-Hard, is specifically about math problems: it evaluates how well LLMs solve high-school and university-level math problems. It uses 1,324 highest difficulty problems (Level 5) from the Hendrycks MATH dataset spread across 7 topics (precalculus, prealgebra, algebra, intermediate algebra, counting/probability and number theory), using a 5-shot approach (the model is provided with 5 examples in the prompt to showcase how it should answer).

In the leaderboard, models would have to end their answers with a very specific string (following the Minerva-Math paper):

The leaderboard would then try to parse [ANSWER] with SymPy to convert it to a symbolic representation (and simplify the values if needed), before finally comparing it to the gold target.

However, users reported a number of issues with the above.

To start, a recurring issue was the inability of some models to follow the expected answer format from the examples: they outputted other sentences instead to introduce their answers. Since the format was not followed, answers were marked as wrong even if they were actually correct! (Which is an issue if what you’re interested in is “how good the model is at math” specifically).

The next step, converting [ANSWER] to the symbolic representation also presented some issues, this time linked to the SymPy parsing:

On the final step, when comparing the extracted answer with the target expression, a number of issues also occurred:

All of these issues are now completely fixed with the new Math-Verify parser!

As all these issues tend to accumulate, some models deeply suffered from this, and their performance was strongly underestimated… so we removed the previous evaluator and added Math-Verify, which was as simple as changing only 3 lines of code! (You can try it too on your math evals!)

This therefore meant re-evaluating all submitted models since June… and it completely overhauled the top 20 models on the MATH subset of the leaderboard.

On average, models solved 61 more problems across the board, equating to a 4.66-point increase across the board!

The two subsets that showed the most significant improvement were both algebra-related (Algebra and Prealgebra) with gains of 8.27 and 6.93, respectively. In extreme cases, some models demonstrated improvements of nearly 90 points on these subsets. We believe these subsets saw the greatest improvement because they frequently involve answers presented as sets (due to questions with multiple solutions) and matrices. The Math-Verify has enhanced its handling of both answer types, contributing to these notable gains.

We initially discovered the math evaluation issues when inspecting Qwen models, which had unusually low scores compared to the self-reported performance. After the Math-Verify introduction, the scores more than doubled for these models, showcasing previous severe underestimation of performance.

But Qwen models aren’t alone. Another major family affected is DeepSeek. After switching to Math-Verify, DeepSeek models almost tripled their scores! This is because their answers are typically wrapped in boxed (\boxed{}) notations which the old evaluator couldn’t extract.

As mentioned at the beginning, the Top 20 rankings have undergone a significant shift, with Nvidia’s AceMath models now dominating the MATH-Hard leaderboard. Other major beneficiaries of this change are the Qwen derivatives, which are now almost exclusively the only models ranking right below AceMath. Following is the complete table comparing the old and new Top 20 leaderboard rankings:

Finally, we examined how the overall Leaderboard results have evolved. While the top four positions remain unchanged, the rest have undergone significant shifts. Due to the rise of multiple Qwen derivatives in the MATH subset, the presence of Qwen models among the top 20 has grown-derived models grown even further at the Overall results.

Many other models also completely jumped in the rankings, gaining 200 places or more! You can check out the results in more detail at the Open LLM Leaderboard.

The introduction of Math-Verify has significantly improved the accuracy and fairness of our evaluations on the Open LLM Leaderboard. This has led to a reshuffling of the leaderboard, with many models showing substantial improvements in their scores.

We encourage all developers and researchers to adopt Math-Verify for their own math evaluations. By doing so, you can ensure that your models are evaluated with more reliable results. Additionally, we invite you to explore the updated rankings and see how your favorite models have changed in performance.

Track, rank and evaluate open LLMs and chatbots

#10868. Top 6 AI Video Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame. Today several tools produce 1080p or even 4K clips with synchronized audio, camera control and reference-based consistency. The market also moves quickly: OpenAI announced it was shutting down Sora in March 2026, so the list of tools worth using has changed.

This guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today. For each one you will see what it does well, where it falls short and who it suits. Plans, credits and model names change often, so confirm details on each vendor’s site before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI video generator puts a range of video models behind one interface. Its page lists models such as Veo 3.1, Kling, Seedance, Wan, Hailuo and PixVerse, so you can run the same prompt on different engines and compare the results without managing separate accounts.

Beyond text-to-video and image-to-video, it offers start and end frame control, video-to-video restyling, motion transfer from a reference clip, a character builder for consistency, lip sync and conversational editing for tasks such as swapping a background or relighting a scene. Resolution goes up to 4K on many models, with 1080p as the default, and clips are usually up to 15 seconds, with longer limits on a few models.

Strengths: model variety, a single credit pool, editing tools alongside generation and a shared library for your clips.

Limits: credit use varies by model, so it is worth testing short clips first. Commercial-use rights depend on your plan and on the model you pick, so check the pricing and terms pages.

Best for: creators and small teams that want to compare models quickly instead of committing to one.

Veo is Google DeepMind’s video model. Veo 3.1 generates sound effects, ambient noise and dialogue together with the video, supports image-to-video, first and last frame transitions, reference images for characters or objects, and outputs 1080p and 4K. You can reach it through the Gemini app, Google Flow and the Gemini API.

Strengths: audio generated with the picture, strong prompt adherence and an API that fits into developer workflows.

Limits: base clips are short, around 8 seconds, so longer scenes rely on scene extension. Dialogue quality in short segments is still being refined, and access and quotas depend on your Google plan.

Best for: developers and marketers who want audio and video from one prompt, or who plan to automate generation through an API.

Runway has been a staple of AI filmmaking since its early Gen models. Its pricing page lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph alongside partner models, and the paid plans include all video and image models, 4K upscaling and parallel generations. Higher tiers add features such as voice clones, brand kits and HDR or ProRes output.

Strengths: polished editing tools, video-to-video workflows and a professional output pipeline that suits post-production teams.

Limits: credits are consumed quickly on premium models, and on the lower paid plans they do not roll over from month to month.

Best for: video editors and agencies that need control over shots and want AI to fit into an existing editing process.

Kling from Kuaishou has built a reputation for natural motion and expressive characters. The current release, Kling 4.0, sits alongside tools such as Motion Control, a canvas workspace, an agent and MCP or CLI batch generation for teams that want to automate production.

Strengths: realistic movement, motion transfer and batch tools for producing many short clips.

Limits: the main site does not spell out all clip-length and resolution limits for each model, so check the model page you plan to use. Pricing and free credits vary by region and plan.

Best for: social video, product shots and character-driven clips where motion quality is the priority.

Luma’s Dream Machine is built on the Ray model family. Its current page lists Ray3.2 and Ray3.14, along with a “Modify video” tool that restyles footage, extends duration and reframes aspect ratios. It also lists camera-motion controls and high-quality EXR export for professional pipelines.

Strengths: reshooting or restyling existing footage, camera-motion control and pipeline-friendly export.

Limits: paid plans start at around $30 per month (or less when billed yearly), and heavy use pushes you into the higher tiers.

Best for: filmmakers and designers who want to modify and extend footage rather than only generate new clips.

Adobe Firefly offers text-to-video and image-to-video with Adobe’s own Firefly Video Model. It also provides partner models, including Google Veo 3.1, Luma Ray3, Kling and Runway Gen-4.5, so you can compare outputs from inside one product. An Assembler and AI video editor let you trim, reorder, extend and add voiceovers, music and sound effects.

Adobe states that the Firefly Video Model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain material, and describes its output as safe for commercial use. Partner models may carry different terms, so read the details for whichever model you choose.

Strengths: a clear licensing story for the native model, integration with Adobe’s creative apps and an included editor.

Limits: most clips run up to 8 seconds, with some models reaching 15. Credits are allocated monthly, and premium partner models can use them faster.

Best for: brand and in-house teams that care about provenance and already work in Adobe tools.

The table summarizes what each vendor’s own pages say at the time of writing. “Entry paid plan” figures are US prices billed annually where the vendor offers that option.

Credit counts are hard to compare, so convert them to clips. Runway’s pricing page lists Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per 5-second clip, which means the 625 monthly credits on the Standard plan cover roughly ten clips. Adobe says its Standard plan’s 2,000 credits equal up to 40 five-second videos, and OpenArt’s Starter plan lists about 50 videos for 4,000 credits. Premium models cost more: the same Runway page lists Aleph 2.0 at 140 credits per 5 seconds.

Plan for waste. If you keep one usable clip out of every three attempts, your real cost per finished shot is about three times the sticker price. Test with short, low-resolution drafts, then render the winner at full quality.

Because every tool outputs short clips, the real work is assembly. A typical workflow is: write a shot list, generate two or three takes per shot, pick the best, normalize them to one format, join them and add captions and audio. FFmpeg handles the joining step from the command line:

Matching resolution, frame rate and codec before joining avoids glitches at the cut points. For character consistency across shots, reuse the same reference image in every prompt and keep descriptions of the subject identical.

If the clip ends up on your own site, treat it like any other media. Provide a poster image, load metadata only until the visitor presses play, and include captions so deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and anyone watching without sound, can follow along. The W3C’s guidance on captions and subtitles explains what to include, and the MDN video element reference covers the attributes below.

Also write a text description or transcript near the video. Search engines and screen reader users cannot see the footage, so the surrounding text is what explains it.

Short, structured prompts beat long, vague ones. Describe the elements in the order a director would:

Change one element at a time between takes so you can tell which change improved the result.

Marketing demos show the best of a tool, so run your own test. Use the same prompt, duration and aspect ratio on each tool, generate a few takes and score them against a short checklist. Keep notes on how many credits each usable clip costs.

Run the same test again with an image-to-video input if your workflow starts from product photos or illustrations. That often exposes differences in consistency that text prompts hide.

Which AI video generator is best? There is no single winner. Veo is strong for audio, Runway for editing, Kling for motion, Luma for modifying footage and Firefly for licensing clarity. A multi-model tool such as OpenArt helps you compare them.

Can AI video generators make long videos? Not in one pass. Most models create short clips, so longer videos are built by extending or stitching clips together.

Is Sora still available? OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it was shutting down the Sora app and API, so it is not a safe choice for new projects.

Can I use AI videos commercially? Often, but it depends on the plan and the underlying model. Read the current terms before publishing.

How do I keep a character consistent across clips? Reuse the same reference image, keep the subject description identical in every prompt, and use character or reference tools where the platform offers them.

Should I add captions to AI-generated video? Yes. Captions help accessibility and viewers watching without sound, and they give search engines text to index.

Do I need a powerful computer? No. These services run in the cloud, so a browser and a stable connection are enough.

The best AI video generator depends on what you make. Start with a short test prompt, compare a few tools, and keep the one that gives you usable clips at a sensible credit cost. If you are not sure where to begin, a multi-model option such as OpenArt lets you try several engines before you settle on one.

#10866. Introducing Three New Serverless Inference Providers: Hyperbolic, Nebius AI Studio, and Novita 🔥

We’re thrilled to announce the addition of three more outstanding serverless Inference Providers to the Hugging Face Hub: Hyperbolic, Nebius AI Studio, and Novita. These providers join our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. #10865. 7 E-commerce UX Tips for Selling Car Accessories and Home & Kitchen Products Online

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

A phone mount on a white background says nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

Mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

If your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

What are the most important e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

How should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

How big should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

How can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

Good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.

#10864. PaliGemma 2 Mix - New Instruction Vision Language Models by Google

Last December, Google released PaliGemma 2: a new family of pre-trained (pt) PaliGemma vision language models (VLMs) based on SigLIP and Gemma 2. The models come in three different sizes (3B, 10B, 28B) and three different resolutions (224x224, 448x448, 896x896).

Today, Google is releasing PaliGemma 2 mix: fine-tuned on a mix of vision language tasks, including OCR, long and short captioning and more.

PaliGemma 2 pretrained (pt) variants are great vision language models to transfer on a given task at hand. All pt checkpoints are meant to be fine-tuned on a downstream task and were released for that purpose.

The mix models give a quick idea of the performance one would get when fine-tuning the pre-trained checkpoints on a downstream task. The main purpose of the PaliGemma model family is to provide pretrained models that can learn better on a downstream task, instead of providing a versatile chat model. Mix models give a good signal of how pt models perform when fine-tuned on a mix of academic datasets.

You can read more about PaliGemma 2 in this blog post.

You can find all the mix models and the demo in this collection.

PaliGemma 2 mix models can accomplish a variety of tasks. We can categorize them according to their subtasks as follows.

Note that this list of subtasks is non-exhaustive, and you can get more information on the full list of tasks in the PaliGemma 2 paper.

When prompting PaliGemma 2 mix models, we can use open-ended prompts. In the previous iteration of PaliGemma pretrained models, we needed to add a task prefix to the prompt depending on the task we’d like to accomplish in a given language. This still works, but open-ended prompts yield better performance. Prompts with task prefix look like the following:

Only two tasks that work solely with task prefixes are object detection and image segmentation. The prompts look like the following.

We have evaluated PaliGemma 2 mix variants according to their localization-related capabilities. Given a prompt “detect {object description};{another object description}” with different objects of interest, PaliGemma can detect different objects of interest. The prompt here is not limited to short classes like “bird,” but it can be “bird on a stick”.

Below, you can find detection and segmentation outputs of different variants with a fixed resolution of 448x448. We zoom in on the object of interest for visualization purposes.

#10863. SmolVLM2: Bringing Video Understanding to Every Device

SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere. Our goal is simple: make video understanding accessible across all devices and use cases, from phones to servers.

We are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero. We've made all models and demos available in this collection.

Want to try SmolVLM2 right away? Check out our interactive chat interface where you can test visual and video understanding capabilities of SmolVLM2 2.2B through a simple, intuitive interface.

We are introducing three new models with 256M, 500M and 2.2B parameters. The 2.2B model is the go-to choice for vision and video tasks, while the 500M and 256M models represent the smallest video language models ever released.

While they're small in size, they outperform any existing models per memory consumption. Looking at Video-MME (the go-to scientific benchmark in video), SmolVLM2 joins frontier model families on the 2B range and we lead the pack in the even smaller space.

Video-MME stands out as a comprehensive benchmark due to its extensive coverage across diverse video types, varying durations (11 seconds to 1 hour), multiple data modalities (including subtitles and audio), and high-quality expert annotations spanning 900 videos totaling 254 hours. Learn more here.

Compared with the previous SmolVLM family, our new 2.2B model got better at solving math problems with images, reading text in photos, understanding complex diagrams, and tackling scientific visual questions. This shows in the model performance across different benchmarks:

When it comes to video tasks, 2.2B is a good bang for the buck. Across the various scientific benchmarks we evaluated it on, we want to highlight its performance on Video-MME where it outperforms all existing 2B models.

We were able to achieve a good balance on video/image performance thanks to the data mixture learnings published in Apollo: An Exploration of Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models

It’s so memory efficient, that you can run it even in a free Google Colab.

Nobody dared to release such small video models until today.

Our new SmolVLM2-500M-Video-Instruct model has video capabilities very close to SmolVLM 2.2B, but at a fraction of the size: we're getting the same video understanding capabilities with less than a quarter of the parameters 🤯.

And then there's our little experiment, the SmolVLM2-256M-Video-Instruct. Think of it as our "what if" project - what if we could push the boundaries of small models even further? Taking inspiration from what IBM achieved with our base SmolVLM-256M-Instruct a few weeks ago, we wanted to see how far we could go with video understanding. While it's more of an experimental release, we're hoping it'll inspire some creative applications and specialized fine-tuning projects.

To demonstrate our vision in small video models, we've built three practical applications that showcase the versatility of these models.

We make SmolVLM2 available to use with transformers and MLX from day zero. In this section, you can find different inference alternatives and tutorials for video and multiple images.

The easiest way to run inference with the SmolVLM2 models is through the conversational API – applying the chat template takes care of preparing all inputs automatically.

You can pass videos through a chat template by passing in {"type": "video", "path": {video_path}. See below for a complete example.

In addition to video, SmolVLM2 supports multi-image conversations. You can use the same API through the chat template, providing each image using a filesystem path, an URL, or a PIL.Image object:

Then you can run inference on a single image using the following one-liner, which uses the unquantized 500M version of SmolVLM2:

We also created a simple script for video understanding. You can use it as follows:

Note that the system prompt is important to bend the model to the desired behaviour. You can use it to, for example, describe all scenes and transitions, or to provide a one-sentence summary of what's going on.

The Swift language is also supported through the mlx-swift-examples repo, which is what we used to build our iPhone app.

Until our in-progress PR is finalized and merged, you have to compile the project from this fork, and then you can use the llm-tool CLI on your Mac as follows.

Video analysis is also supported, as well as providing a system prompt. We found system prompts to be particularly helpful for video understanding, to drive the model to the desired level of detail we are interested in. This is a video inference example:

You can fine-tune SmolVLM2 on videos using transformers 🤗 We have fine-tuned the 500M variant in Colab on video-caption pairs in VideoFeedback dataset for demonstration purposes. Since the 500M variant is small, it's better to apply full fine-tuning instead of QLoRA or LoRA, meanwhile you can try to apply QLoRA on cB variant. You can find the fine-tuning notebook here.

#10862. Top 6 AI YouTube Transcript Generators: Features, Accuracy, and Limits

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

There is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Is it legal to transcribe someone else's YouTube video? Transcribing for personal research or accessibility is common, but republishing the text may infringe copyright. Check the video's license and YouTube's terms, and get permission when in doubt.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#10861. SigLIP 2: A better multilingual vision language encoder

Today Google releases a new and better family of multilingual vision-language encoders, SigLIP 2. The authors have extended the training objective of SigLIP (sigmoid loss) with additional objectives for improved semantic understanding, localization, and dense features.

SigLIP 2 models outperform the older SigLIP ones at all model scales in core capabilities, including zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and transfer performance when extracting visual representations for Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

A cherry on top is the dynamic resolution (naflex) variant. This is useful for downstream tasks sensitive to aspect ratio and resolution.

Here is a list of all the models released:

Vision encoders are simple - they take an image, encode it into a representation, and that representation is used for downstream tasks like classification, object detection, image segmentation, and more vision tasks. Researchers are always in pursuit of visual representations that are dense, locality-aware, and semantically rich.

CLIP and ALIGN are the first examples of image encoders and text encoders aligned together through joint training. This approach opened new ways to train vision models. SigLIP took it further, replacing CLIP's contrastive loss with sigmoid loss for even better encoders.

The takeaway? With smarter training objectives, we keep building vision encoders that are more structured, fine-grained, and powerful. SigLIP 2 is just that, a bunch of really interesting and smart training objectives applied on top of that of SigLIP's to provide better and stronger vision language encoders.

We will try something new with this blog post. Rather than stating what is new and where to find it, we will go through a little exercise together. We start off with SigLIP and then brainstorm a series of questions (prefixed with 🤔) and answers (a new heading) to gradually cover all the updates in SigLIP 2. Sounds good?

We will begin our journey with the vision encoder where the patch size is 16, and the image resolution is 256. We have four variants to start our training:

🤔 Question 1: What is a (low effort) auxiliary training objective that we can use to learn better visual representations (in terms of location awareness and sense of locality)?

Let’s add a decoder to the mix. Now we have an image encoder, a text encoder, and a text decoder. The text decoder will have three objectives:

The decoder provides an additional signal to the vision encoder, making it location-aware. This marks the first improvement to the training recipe in SigLIP 2.

🤔 Question 2: How do we improve fine-grained local semantics of the image representation?

To improve fine-grained local semantics in image representation, we introduce two key training objectives, Global-Local Loss, and Masked Prediction Loss. Taking inspiration from self-supervised learning literature, we use self-distillation. We can use a model as a teacher, and the same model as a student. Upon each iteration the teacher will be the moving average of the student's parameters.

These objectives teach the vision encoder to be spatially aware and improve its local semantics. The authors add this loss only after 80% of the training is done with the sigmoid and decoder loss. This is done in order to save compute (additional losses are pretty expensive) and to not negatively affect the encoders.

🤔 Question 3: How to adapt models to different resolutions?

It is a known fact that image models can be very sensitive to varying resolutions and aspect ratios. Here we can leverage two distinct methodologies to adapt these models on different resolutions and patch sizes.

Models with the -naflex suffix are the dynamic resolution variants. While the fixed-resolution models can be used out of the box with the existing SiglipModel class, you would need to use Siglip2Model to use the naflex variants. We handle this automatically when you use the pipeline API!

This brings us to the end of the evolution from SigLIP to SigLIP 2. In the next sections we will look at applications with SigLIP 2.
